children.text: [On screen: Black and white portrait of a young Americo Paredes]

Then in 54, I went with a tape recorder, a very primitive tape recorder. It weighed something like 60 pounds. [laughs] I had to carry that. I had to do it where there was a good current. For example, I used--
Hard to find. It was difficult to find I imagine, good current. Electricity was difficult to find [laughter].

Only on the American side. When I worked on the Mexican side. I had a different tape recorder. In fact, we just gave it away or threw it away. It was not as heavy. I used it to tape record people in Mexico City. When I came back, I couldn't understand it because the power,
[On screen: Black and white photo of an older Americo Paredes holding the Charles Frankel Prize, 11-16-1989]
it was alternate current, I think. Is that the one? The power was so low. What they did here, they put it at that particular speed. They can do wonders.

They re-recorded it so one understands what's being said. I recorded the great Mexican folklorist Vicente Mendoza and other people. Getting their biographies and things, more or less what you're doing here. [laughter] Without all this wonderful equipment. [laughter]
You still have those tapes?
They're somewhere in Sid Richardson Hall. The best thing I did with them was recording music. They were reel-to-reel tapes and they were supposed to be rewound,
[On screen: The back-side of the black and white photo of an older Americo Paredes holding the Charles Frankel Prize, 11-16-1989]
I think, every six months or every year. I don't think they ever did it. Some people have used them, but I'm sure that as for quality, it isn't there.
[On screen: Black and white photo of Americo Paredes and his wife]
Because I was recording in houses, out in the open, in cantinas, so the sound wasn't any good, but it was good enough for me to be able to transcribe the tunes. I had the words as well.
What were the cantinas like? Lively?
One of them where I took Bill Cohens and he forgot about it. I think it's called Las Dos Repúblicas now, it's a fancy place. Then it had sawdust on the floor.
Just for pure research right Doctor Paredes? just for research.

Just for research. [laughter] It was right down in the marketplace. It was not in Boys Town. [laughter] You could smell the urinals. [laughter] It was a men's cantina. I remember I took Cohens in there and they played El Corrido de Cortez. A bunch of drunken rancheros,

they would come up to Cohens. In Spanish they would say, "Ese era hombre gringo, el tal por cual". [Translation: "That was a gringo man, the so-and-so".] He couldn't understand a word so they smiled at him and he smiled back. [laughter]
When they finished, I told Bill, "Let's get out of here." I got him out of there. I told him, "You were in some danger," "You're just trying to put me on." He never believed. But he was.
[laughs] Ese era hombre gringo. [laughter]

Some people, especially people from southern Mexico, Have a way of talking, in a very low voice they smile as they shoot you or stick a knife in- [laughter] They know when they're fighting each other, they know that they're being hostile. Poor Bill didn't know.
I think that's what really kept him from at least getting pushed around or hit with a bottle or something, that he just smiled back.
See, that goes back to the importance of being bilingual. Right?
Right. [laughter]
[On screen: Black and white photo Americo Paredes in his cap and gown when he received his PhD]

children.text: Is this on the day of your graduation?

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: I don't remember. I think Lorenzo lent you another one where- That's one, individual where you're there. Yes. That is for the PhD. Because I was so busy getting first a Bachelor's then the Master's, I didn't attend graduation ceremonies for the Bachelor's or for the Master's.

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: I did go for the PhD. That's for the PhD.

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: Is this a new book that's coming out?
[On screen: Color photograph of Americo Paredes’s home on Van Buren Street.]
It's a reprint. This book was published by the University of Illinois Press. The UT Press just bought the rights and they're reprinting it.  Behind that photograph is the address.
Yes, it’s Van Buren correct?
[On screen: Back-side of photo reads, Sept. 14, 1980. 1442 East Van Buren St. Brownsville, Texas.]
I think that house is still there.
[inaudible]
I wrote it down [inaudible].
Do you recall barely doing an address there or a presentation?
No, this was when I retired in 1984. Because I recognize some of the people that look like Nancy Langford, the wife of one of my colleagues. I think I was telling a joke there. [laughter]
[On screen: Black and white photograph of Americo Paredes at a podium speaking]
Lorenzo had a- He remembers you wrote a book of poems, I think, in the 1930s, and he remembers you with a hat and a tie. Do you have a photograph?

I destroyed all the copies of that book I’ve been able to get my hands on. It was very bad poetry and even that-- You know this columnist, Calvin Trilling, I think, who has this picture with his hat on. I think he does it as a joke. I did it seriously in 1975, my hat on. [laughter]
So there's no more copies?

Well, I hope not. [laughter] That was for 1984. I retired, really. I could have stayed, but my brother Amador, he just wasted away with cancer, and I couldn't take it. I went through a period of clinical depression for about a year. I retired, left my office, everything.
[On screen: Black and white photograph of Americo Paredes in his office holding a drawing of himself that is part of an award]
Then I came back and taught part-time.
You taught part-time until what year?
It must have been for perhaps starting in 85 to around 88. Then my heart condition got very bad. The doctor told me not to teach anymore.
Do you recall something about this photograph?

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: The university gave me that award. It's up there on the shelf. I can show it to you. Later they came and photographed me in my study, in my office at the university.

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: This award was for what? What was the name of the award?

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: They recognized me just for 25 years of working for the Mexican-American people and so on. Though it was the historians that did it. At that time, I had this mariachi [background noise] and it was a kind of surprise. I gave a short talk and then out comes the mariachi and serenades me, so on.

children.text: [On screen: Black and white photograph of Americo Paredes standing holding a plaque and certificate]

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: You can see we were very activist. You can see in the background is the farm workers' logo, "Viva la raza". [chuckles]

tags.tag: The University of Texas at Austin

children.text: Here's an interesting photograph. It's got 66. Was that the celebration of your birthday?

[inaudible] 66- Kansas[?]. [Background conversation] 
That's Tish Hinojosa here and Manuel Peña, my ex-student. He's a member of the faculty here now.
I got to see him. He was a speaker at the Tejano Music Awards last year in San Antonio.
[On screen: Black and white photograph of an older Americo Paredes playing the guitar]

By the way, I got some plaque also from him at that time. He has a very interesting background, his Bachelor's is in music, his Master's is in English and he worked on Joyce. and his PhD is in Anthropology.
He is a really well-rounded man, a very good guitarist also, though I don't think he's playing anymore. I mean once you get into academic route, there's not much time.
[background conversation]
[On screen: Color photograph of Americo Paredes in a living room sitting down with Manuel Peña and Tish Hinojosa, each playing a guitar]
I hope you'll autograph these for me.

I will be very happy to do so. I would have to tell you that you all won't recognize my name. Arthritis is really-- I used to have a pretty good hand, "I used to do this. I used to do that:" That's what happens when you're pushing 80. I'll be very happy to do so.
[background conversation]

Since we spoke last, Dr. Paredes, I spoke with Pat Jasper and she called Tish Hinojosa. They gave me Mike Crowley's number. It was Tish's manager. I think we're going to get permission to use her song for part of the video that we're making on you as
a conclusion. [crosstalk] [Americo: That's very good.] It's quite a tribute. I wrote them a letter thanking them.
She's a very sweet person, unassuming. I think she's better known abroad than she's here. Although she's getting to be known well.
Most Texas artists are I think [laughter] [inaudible] in Austin or in Texas.
That’s right, that's the way it is. [laughter] No profit in their own country. [laughter] [background conversation]
It's always been that way for years with jazz musicians
You're right.
[background conversation]
Of course, earlier the black musicians had to go to Chicago. [background conversation]
That was a whole cultural news because the cities were opening up as well.
[On screen: Black and white photograph of Americo Paredes and a man walking across the street carrying a coat and a work bag]
That's true. Tish became very popular in Korea, South Korea. Through a very interesting situation that some Korean magnate over there had a TV program and he wanted a song

to use as a beginning and end, and he was here and he liked the song of Tish. So he used it. Apparently, the Koreans became interested in her and started buying her records. I think she had two Platinums in Korea. Incredible. I suppose a lot of them know English already.
They probably had [inaudible] on LPs there. I see these records from Taiwan and Korea and they're always orange vinyl or something.

You're good? That's all I had for a long time and I still have not graduated to CDs because I don't have time to play. Whenever I can play something I stick a little cassette into my old machine and play. I have a turntable.
Yes, I saw the turntable. It's a little high now to use it. [laughter]

I haven't used it for a long time. But I had a lot of old Mexican LPs and an old Louis Armstrong record of-- What's the name of the song? Saint Louis Blues. I couldn't remember the words. He's playing the trumpet.
[On screen: Medal with green and black ribbon, it reads 'Don Jose de Escandon- STHGF - H MAT TAM - 1991']
Okay. Dr. Paredes, could you tell us a little bit about this? This is one of your awards.
The other one was the one that--
you received from the Mexican Government?

The Mexican Government gave me that. Somewhere there's a certificate signed by Salinas de Gortari and a number of others. That was given to four or three of us. Chávez was one of them, César Chávez, but I couldn't go. They went to-- They got it in Mexico City.
So they sent somebody down here and I was going to--
They gave you the award.

The other one, that was given to me by the State of Tamaulipas, that’s the Escandon. Escandón was the founder. Sometime later. 
[On screen: A gold medal with golden ribbon, it is the Order of the Aztec Eagle award featuring a Cuauhtémoc eagle in the center]
[background conversation]
May we move to your study, Dr. Paredes?
Sure. [background conversation]

[On screen: award which reads, Con los atentos saludos de la Dirección General del Protocolo de la Secretaria de Relaciones Exteriores. Translation: With the attentive greetings of the General Directorate of Protocol of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs]
[On screen: Photo of Americo Paredes with his arm around a little girl, and his wife standing behind him]
They have you working.
[On screen: Black and white photo of a young Americo Paredes reading documents at his desk]
Someone’s got to work. Es fácil lo que estoy haciendo. [Translation: It’s easy what I’m doing.]
He is strumming on the guitar over there. What chance can you get your video camera set up over there?
[Americo plays guitar] I better not.
Try it, please. What was your favorite song when you sang in the radio?
If I try to bring it up to who it should be I think the strings-
It's very old.
We can tune it down maybe, instead of up.
Can we try that?
[Americo plays guitar] ... I think it's even. [inaudible] beginning to lie [inaudible] mentir. [laughs].
[Americo plays guitar] ... [inaudible] ...very old.
[Americo plays guitar] ... [video cuts to black]
